{{Short description|Japanese mathematician}}
{{family name hatnote|Wada|lang=Japanese}}

{{nihongo|'''Wada Yenzō Nei'''|和田 寧||1787 &ndash; October 13, 1840}}, also known as '''Wada Yasushi''', was a Japanese [[mathematician]] in the [[Edo period]].  His birth name was Kōyama Naoaki; but he changed his name to Wada Nei, by which he became more widely known.<ref>Smith, David. (1914). {{Google books|J1YNAAAAYAAJ|''A History of Japanese Mathematics,'' pp. 220-229. |page=220}}</ref>

==Life and work==
Wada studied under the patronage of the hereditary  {{nihongo|Chief court calendar-maker|暦博士|Reki-hakase}}<ref>Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). {{Google books|Cg8oAAAAMAAJ|''Annales des empereur du japon,'' p. 427.|page=427}}</ref>  in the court of the emperor.<ref>Restivo, Sal P. (1992). {{Google books|gvMm0jv-xPIC|''Mathematics in Society and History: Sociological Inquiries,'' p. 59.|page=59}}</ref>

Wada became a student of [[Kusaka Sei]], who had been a student of [[Ajima Chokuyen]]. Wada extended [[Ajima Chokuyen]]'s development of an integral calculus within the [[Enri]] ({{lang|ja-Hani|円理}}, "circle principle") context. He worked on the computation of [[Maxima and minima|minimum and maximum values]] (roughly by [[equation|equating]] the first [[derivate|derivative]] to 0) and gave reasoning and insight to the computation method that was given without explanation by [[Seki Takakazu]] about 100 years earlier. He was also the first Japanese mathematician to study [[Roulette (curve)|roulettes]].

==Selected works==
Wada's published writings are few.<ref>[http://www.oclc.org/research/activities/identities/default.htm  WorldCat Identities]: [http://www.worldcat.org/identities/lccn-nr96-28101   Wada Yasushi 和田寧 1787-1840]</ref>
